places.name: Old Shasta
places.text: Highway 299 leads to Shasta, about six miles west of Redding. In the 1850s it was the largest town in the area and the county seat, home to some 3,500 people. Then in 1873 the railroad bypassed it for Redding, and Shasta faded into a near ghost town. Its row of Gold Rush brick buildings is now a state historic park.
places.more: State Parks calls it the Queen City of California's northern mining district. It was a major shipping point for the mule trains and stagecoaches that served the mining towns of northern California. Shasta lost the county seat to Redding in 1888. Its courthouse has been restored to the way it looked in 1861 and now holds exhibits and a collection of historic California art. It also has a Masonic lodge described as the oldest in California. Poet Joaquin Miller wrote about being jailed here for horse stealing and escaping with help from his Native American wife. The 2018 Carr Fire destroyed the old elementary school and damaged the cemetery.

places.name: The 9.5-mile conveyor belt
places.text: To make concrete for Shasta Dam, builders needed mountains of sand and gravel. So they built what was then the largest conveyor belt system in the world, 9.5 miles long, running from Redding to the dam site. It could carry 1,100 tons of material an hour.
places.more: The belt rode on some 16,000 rollers and was divided into 26 sections. Twenty-three sections had their own 200-horsepower motors. The other three ran downhill, so they needed no power at all, and builders rigged them to generate electricity for some of the other sections. Over the whole job, the belt hauled more than 12 million tons of rock. At the end of the line, a mixing plant made concrete, and steel buckets holding 8 cubic yards rode cables out from a main tower 465 feet tall. That tower was never fully torn down. It still stands underwater behind the dam and appears when the lake drops low enough.

places.name: Shasta Lake, the dam towns
places.text: The city of Shasta Lake grew out of five small communities that sprang up in 1938, when work began on Shasta Dam: Central Valley, Project City, Summit City, Pine Grove and Toyon. Pine Grove stood where Pine Grove Avenue now meets the freeway. The communities did not join into one city until 1993.
places.more: Toyon, first called Government Camp, was built by the Bureau of Reclamation on what had been the Seaman Ranch. Everyone who lived there worked for the Bureau. By 1950 it had two tennis courts, green lawns, concrete sidewalks and its own sewage plant. Bureau employees had to leave by the end of 1964, and the camp became a Job Corps site until 1972. Local Native Americans then occupied Toyon, hoping to have it recognized as tribal land, but that never happened. Many of the homes later burned. Today a metal storage building and a flagpole are all that remain, on a fenced-off site along Shasta Dam Boulevard.

places.name: Shasta Dam
places.text: Shasta Dam stands about four miles west, 602 feet tall. When it was finished in 1945, 26 months earlier than planned, only Hoover Dam was taller. During World War II, with so many men gone to fight, many of the workers were women and high school students. One workman reportedly summed it up: Old Shasta's about the secondest dam there is.
places.more: Before it was built, it was called Kennett Dam, and it was planned to stand more than 800 feet tall. Wartime shortages of supplies and labor cut it to 602 feet. Even before it was finished, its power plant sent electricity to shipyards and aircraft factories. Chief engineer Frank Crowe, who had run construction at Hoover Dam, declared that the powerhouse would keep making power until somebody discovered how to make power out of sunlight. The dam also cut salmon off from about half of the best salmon habitat in the Sacramento River basin. Tours ride an elevator roughly 400 feet down into the dam.

places.name: Kennett, the drowned town
places.text: Under Shasta Lake lies Kennett, once the largest mining town in the area outside Redding and Shasta. Its two biggest mines held unusually pure copper ore. There's no record of any public hearing to ask residents before it was flooded. By 1944 the whole town was underwater, and it now sits under roughly 400 feet of water, depending on the lake level.
places.more: The town site lies in the homeland of the Wintu people, who called the place Munuktsiraw. Gold was found on Backbone Creek here in 1852. The town was named for a railroad man known as Squire Kennet, and the second t may have come from a mapmaker's mistake. Kennett boomed during World War I, when metal prices were high. Its biggest mine, the Mammoth, closed for good in 1923, and the town lost its city status in 1931. The groundbreaking ceremony for Shasta Dam was held in Kennett in 1937.

places.name: The drowned highway
places.text: Before the lake, old Highway 99 ran through Mountain Gate and then plunged into the valley that Shasta Lake now fills. In drought years, when the water falls, old bridges, road cuts and guardrails come back into view.
places.more: When the dam went in, both the highway and the Southern Pacific railroad had to move east onto a brand-new, much higher bridge over the Pit River. The old railroad track from Redding toward the dam site became a branch line for construction trains. At the dam site, a railroad tunnel was cleared and reshaped to carry the whole Sacramento River around the work. Once the river was diverted, crews could build the middle of the dam, where the spillway sits. The lake began filling in February 1944, when that diversion tunnel was sealed.

places.name: Shasta Lake
places.text: Shasta Lake is California's largest reservoir, with 365 miles of steep, wooded shoreline. It has four big arms, made by the Sacramento River, the McCloud River, the Pit River and Sulanharas Creek. At its deepest, it's 517 feet.
places.more: The biggest river flowing into the lake is not the Sacramento but the Pit. Before the dam, the Pit carried about four times as much water as the Sacramento where the two met. It is one of only three rivers in the United States that cross the Cascade Range, along with the Klamath and the Columbia. The river is named for the pits its people dug, both for winter homes and as traps for game that came to drink. Their descendants are the Pit River Tribe, eleven bands that live along the river in northeastern California. Bridge Bay is the lake's largest marina, with more than 700 slips and about 100 houseboats for rent.
places.spot: Look for houseboats tied up in the coves and marinas.

places.name: Bass Hill stage road
places.text: Near the Bridge Bay exit stands a marker to the stagecoach days. The California and Oregon stage road crossed the top of Bass Hill here and dropped down to the Pit River, and the hill was a favorite spot for bandit holdups. The marker honors the stage drivers under the title Pioneers Who Held the Ribbons.
places.more: The California and Oregon stage line ran all the way from Sacramento to Portland by 1860, carrying mail and passengers every day. In winter it switched to sleighs to get over the Scott Mountains. In 1870 the line changed its route to bypass the old town of Shasta and follow the Sacramento River canyon instead. The stages kept running until the railroad replaced them in 1887. The marker went up in 1920, and the site is California Historical Landmark No. 148.

places.name: Pit River Bridge
places.text: The Pit River Bridge is a double-decker. I-5 rides the top deck and the railroad runs underneath, including Amtrak's Coast Starlight. Built in 1942, it stands about 500 feet above the old bed of the Pit River, making it the highest double-deck bridge in the United States. When the lake is full, though, the water comes within about 40 feet of the bridge.
places.more: On May 3, 1953, back when this was a two-lane highway, a produce truck's steering failed on the bridge. The cab smashed through the railing and dangled over the water with two men trapped inside. Walter Schau and other drivers found a rope and pulled the driver up, with Schau at one point hanging by his ankles. When the cab caught fire, Schau climbed down and pulled out the second man just before it fell into the water. His wife, Virginia, grabbed her Kodak Brownie and took two pictures, the last on her roll. Her photo won the 1954 Pulitzer Prize for Photography, the first ever won by a woman.
places.spot: Look for the lake's water on both sides of the bridge.

places.name: The giant median
places.text: Just north of the Pit River Bridge, the two directions of I-5 split apart, leaving what is said to be the second-largest median in California. Only Interstate 8's In-Ko-Pah grade has a bigger one.
places.more: From Red Bluff all the way to the Oregon line, this road carries a nickname: the Cascade Wonderland Highway. North of Redding it regularly gets snow at higher elevations from fall to spring. Caltrans sometimes requires chains or snow tires, and checkpoints are often set up to enforce the rules. In winter, trucks must carry chains whether or not chain controls are in force.

places.name: Shasta salamanders
places.text: The limestone hills around this lake hide salamanders found nowhere else on Earth. Scientists once thought there was just one kind. In 2018 they found three, including the Wintu Shasta salamander, which lives on the lake's north shore near the McCloud River.
places.more: The three species look so alike that only their ranges and their genes tell them apart. The Samwel Shasta salamander lives on the north-central and northwest sides of the lake. They favor damp limestone cracks and caves, where females lay their eggs. Building the dam and filling the lake probably broke their small range into pieces. Raising the lake higher would flood even more of their homes, and limestone quarrying is another threat. In 2021, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service found that they did not warrant Endangered Species Act protection.

places.name: Lake Shasta Caverns
places.text: Getting to these limestone caves takes a catamaran ride across the lake's McCloud arm and then a bus ride up a steep mountain road. The caves sit about 900 feet above the lake. Inside, the words James Richardson wrote on the wall on November 11, 1878, claiming the discovery, are still clearly legible.
places.more: Richardson worked for the federal fish hatchery on the McCloud River, and the caves were once called Baird Cave, after U.S. Fisheries Commissioner Spencer Fullerton Baird. The caverns were already part of life for the Wintu people, who lived in the area. Until 1964, only a few hardy cavers squeezed in, through a hole in the ceiling barely big enough for one person. To open the caves to visitors, workers blasted a tunnel into the mountain and broke into a room nobody knew about, now called the Discovery Room. It contains every type of limestone formation found there. In 2012 the caverns became a National Natural Landmark. The exit is at O'Brien, named for Con O'Brien, who ran a resort here.

places.name: Winnemem Wintu homeland
places.text: The McCloud River arm of this lake is the homeland of the Winnemem Wintu, whose name means middle water people or middle river people. When the lake filled, scores of their village sites, burial grounds and sacred places went underwater. The Winnemem are still here. They have long sought federal recognition, and they oppose plans to raise the dam.
places.more: In 1854, settlers killed 42 Winnemem men, women and children at Kabyai Creek on the McCloud River. In 1941, Congress passed a law to take Winnemem homes and lands for the Central Valley Project. Winnemem men who came home from World War II in 1945 found their families driven from their villages by the rising water. More than 90 percent of their land was lost. In 2004 the Winnemem held a war dance against raising the dam, which they said was the first since 1887. The Winnemem healer Florence Jones led a successful fight against a new ski resort on Mount Shasta, which the tribe holds sacred.

places.name: The Salt Fire
places.text: On June 30, 2021, a fire started beside I-5 near the Salt Creek exit and shut down the freeway. Forest officials believe it was likely sparked by hot material that fell from a vehicle on the interstate. It destroyed 27 homes and 14 other buildings around Lakehead.
places.more: The fire broke out during a long heat wave, in brush left dry by drought. Within two hours it had grown past 200 acres, and by evening it covered about 1,000. Some residents on Gregory Creek Road were told to shelter at Gregory Creek Beach. The freeway reopened the next morning, and firefighters built their lines near the interstate to keep it open. The fire then burned into land scarred by the Hirz and Delta fires of 2018. It was fully contained on July 19.

places.name: The first federal fish hatchery
places.text: In 1872, the nation's first federal fish hatchery opened on the McCloud River, which now flows into this lake. Livingston Stone built it at a spot where he found Wintu people catching Chinook salmon. Its eggs were shipped across the country and as far as Japan and New Zealand.
places.more: Stone wrote that when his crew arrived, Wintu people gathered with bows and arrows on the far bank and spent a whole day trying to drive them off. Stone later gave the spawned salmon back to the tribe as food, hired Wintu workers until 1883, and wrote that it would be an inhuman outrage to drive them from the river. His reports also used insulting words for them. A few years later he started a second station upriver for rainbow trout, and its eggs went all over the country. Many rainbow trout in the world's waters today descend from McCloud River fish. The McCloud's salmon run declined after a railroad was built nearby in the 1880s.

places.name: Lakehead, top of the lake
places.text: Lakehead sits on the northern shore of Shasta Lake. About 470 people lived here in 2020, and in summer more than 1,500 seasonal residents can join them. In 1992, Caltrans finished upgrading a final 13-mile stretch of I-5 north of Lakehead.
places.more: The lake reaches 15.3 miles up the old Sacramento River channel. Antlers Marina is the northernmost marina on Shasta Lake. The lake is part of the Whiskeytown-Shasta-Trinity National Recreation Area, run by the Shasta-Trinity National Forest. From 1996 through 1999, the lake hosted Boardstock, a wakeboarding event that drew about 15,000 people a year.

places.name: Delta, end of the line
places.text: When the railroad pushed up this canyon in the 1880s, the town of Delta was the end of the line for about two years. Lots sold for 45 to 185 dollars, and almost overnight there were saloons, hotels, a Wells Fargo office and a turntable for the engines. The 39-mile train ride to Redding took two hours and 20 minutes.
places.more: Many people kept calling the place Dog Creek, after a mining town founded in 1855 a few miles west. In 1887 the tracks moved on up the canyon, and Delta slowly emptied out; its post office closed in 1954. Gold mining went on for decades, and one company even ran its own narrow-gauge railroad six and a half miles to the main line. The old one-room Delta school, since enlarged, is one of the few buildings still standing. In September 2018, the Delta Fire started near Lakehead, jumped I-5 and closed the freeway from September 5 to September 10.

places.name: The upper Sacramento River
places.text: The river beside the freeway is the Sacramento, the largest river in California. From its beginnings near Mount Shasta, it runs about 400 miles to San Francisco Bay. Up here it is a blue ribbon trout stream, where wild rainbow trout abound.
places.more: The Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga named it Rio de los Sacramentos in 1808. The upper river starts where its North, Middle and South forks meet near Mount Shasta, then flows into Lake Siskiyou. From there it runs about 60 miles through this canyon, past Dunsmuir and Castella, to Shasta Lake near Lakehead. This stretch supplies about 15 percent of the water flowing into Shasta Lake. For about 12,000 years, people have relied on this river's watershed, which once had one of the densest Native American populations in California.

places.name: Portuguese Flat
places.text: Near the Pollard Flat exit was Portuguese Flat, a Gold Rush camp of the early 1850s made up largely of Portuguese miners. It had rich diggings and a reputation as one of the roughest camps in northern Shasta County. By 1885 it seems to have been deserted, and its site lies along what is now I-5.
places.more: As late as 1933, travelers could still see a few tumbledown buildings, an old log cabin and some aging apple trees here. Ross and Mary Campbell McCloud ran an inn at Portuguese Flat from about 1853 to 1855, before moving on to Upper Soda Springs. In 1855, a young Joaquin Miller was brought to their inn after, by his own account, an arrow pierced his jaw and neck in the Battle of Castle Crags. Mary McCloud nursed him back to health, and Miller went on to become a well-known poet.

places.name: River, rails and road
places.text: The river, the railroad and the freeway all squeeze through this one canyon. The railroad was built up the canyon in the 1880s, along the old Siskiyou Trail. Amtrak's Coast Starlight still runs these tracks every day on its trips between Los Angeles and Seattle.
places.more: From 1949, the Southern Pacific's Shasta Daylight streamliner ran this route between Oakland and Portland in about 15 and a half hours. Writer and train fan Lucius Beebe described riding all morning in the shadowy presence of Mount Shasta, a brooding, symmetrical cone of everlasting snow. When Amtrak took over in 1971, the Southern Pacific's own trains on this route ended, and Dunsmuir became a stop on the Coast Starlight. It is the train's only stop in Siskiyou County and the northernmost passenger station in California. Because of the way the schedules line up, trains in both directions pass through Dunsmuir in the middle of the night.
places.spot: Look for railroad tracks running alongside the river.

places.name: Southern's stage station
places.text: The name of this exit goes back to Simeon Southern, nicknamed Sims, who opened a log stage station and hotel here in 1859, where travelers stopped to rest and eat for 50 years. The settlement of Hazel Creek took the name Sims in 1871, since his station was the center of town. In September 1880, President Rutherford B. Hayes stayed here with Generals Sherman and Sheridan.
places.more: Sims Southern was born on a Kentucky farm in 1822 and reached Shasta County in 1854. He and his wife, Sarah, had ten children and grew the station into a large two-story building. That same September of 1880, the gentleman bandit Black Bart robbed the Yreka to Roseburg stage in Oregon, and three days later Hayes and Sherman rode that very stage. Sarah sold the station to a timber company in 1902, and a sawmill followed. In the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps ran Camp Sims nearby. The site is California Historical Landmark No. 33.

places.name: The Siskiyou Trail
places.text: Long before this was a freeway, it was a web of Native American footpaths between California and the Northwest. In the 1820s, Hudson's Bay Company fur trappers followed them south from the Columbia River, and the route became known as the Siskiyou Trail. I-5 follows the same path today.
places.more: Trapper Alexander McLeod reached the Sacramento River in 1828, and at first the route was called the California Brigade Trail. In 1837, Ewing Young bought hundreds of cattle in Mexican California and drove them up this trail to Oregon, a trip of nearly three months. During that drive, two of his men murdered a Native man. In 1841, a party from the United States Exploring Expedition came down the trail with the region's first scientists and mapmakers. Early travelers on mules and horses managed perhaps 20 miles a day. Toll roads for stagecoaches were not carved through these mountains until the 1860s, and the first telegraph line arrived in 1864.

places.name: Homeland and the 1855 battle
places.text: The country around Castle Crags is the ancestral home of the Okwanuchu Shasta people. The Crags have long been revered by the Wintu, Achumawi and Modoc peoples too, and the area's streams, river and springs are considered sacred. The Gold Rush brought thousands of miners and terrible violence, and in June 1855 miners fought Modoc people below Battle Rock, now marked at the state park entrance.
places.more: Poet Joaquin Miller fought in the battle and later wrote that an arrow went through his jaw and neck. He also wrote about atrocities against Native people, describing a massacre in which a mob of drunken settlers ambushed sleeping women, children and infants. Miners had ruined Modoc fishing places near Lower Soda Springs by filling them with silt from their diggings. False rumors of a fabled Lost Cabin Mine drew even more miners into the Crags. Across California, more than two-thirds of Native people died during the American conquest, from violence and disease. Battle Rock is California Historical Landmark No. 116.

places.name: Castle Crags State Park
places.text: In the 1890s, mineral water from a spring here was bottled and shipped all over the world. The bottling company went broke in the 1929 crash, and in 1943 the state bought 925 acres of the old springs property. That was the start of Castle Crags State Park, which has 28 miles of trails and a vista point facing the Crags and Mount Shasta.
places.more: Native people used the mineral spring long before anyone bottled it. In the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps built a stone enclosure around it, and the water still bubbles up with a sulfur smell. The bottling works was founded in 1889, and George Washington Bailey ran a resort and hotel across the river, with a footbridge to the springs. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake ended plans to develop the area further. Today the Pacific Crest Trail winds through the park, and the Crags Trail climbs to the base of Castle Dome.

places.name: Castle Crags
places.text: These granite spires rise from about 2,000 feet at the river to more than 6,500 feet at the top. The granite formed underground in the Jurassic period, the age of dinosaurs, and Ice Age glaciers later scraped away the softer rock around it. A bellflower that grows here is found nowhere else in the world.
places.more: The rounded hump among the spires is Castle Dome, shaped as huge curved slabs of granite peeled away. California State Parks puts the spires' age at more than 170 million years. A second plant, the Castle Crags ivesia, also grows only here. Much of the Crags lies in the Castle Crags Wilderness, set aside by Congress in 1984. Its northern part has bowls carved by glaciers, and nearby Castle Lake fills the largest one. The granite spires look much like parts of Yosemite.
places.spot: Look for jagged granite spires and a rounded dome above the trees.

places.name: Sleep in a caboose
places.text: Just off this exit, a lodge founded in 1968 lets guests sleep in old cabooses and eat in a restaurant inside an original train car, with Castle Crags towering above. Once called Railroad Park Resort, it now goes by Jubilee Railroad.
places.more: The property covers 43 acres in a forested, spring-fed creek valley. Besides the cabooses, it has vintage cabins and campsites. The lodge calls itself the eastern gateway to the Klamath Knot, a global hot spot for plant and animal variety. Its dining car has outdoor seats where diners can gaze up at the Crags.

places.name: Dunsmuir, the railroad town
places.text: Dunsmuir was a railroad town first, nicknamed Pusher, because extra steam engines were added here to push trains up the steep grades north of town. In 1888, Alexander Dunsmuir, son of a British Columbia coal baron, offered the town a fountain if it would take his name. Its slogan calls it the Home of the Best Water on Earth, filtered through Mount Shasta's lava.
places.more: The first Dunsmuir stop was just a boxcar, farther south. In the early 1900s, Dunsmuir was the largest town in Siskiyou County, and for a long time the largest California city north of Sacramento. When the railroad switched from steam to diesel in the 1950s, it no longer needed so many workers here, and the town shrank. That left downtown looking much as it did in the 1920s and 1930s, and it is now a historic district. The depot houses a railroad museum, and the town still has an operating turntable. Three drinking fountains line Dunsmuir Avenue.

places.name: Upper Soda Springs
places.text: Under the freeway in north Dunsmuir lies Upper Soda Springs, now a riverside park. Okwanuchu people camped here during salmon season, at a wide, shallow spot they called the place to cross the river. In the early 1850s it became home to the area's first non-Native settlers, and later to a toll bridge, a stage hotel and a springhouse serving soda water from the mineral springs.
places.more: Ross and Mary Campbell McCloud built the toll bridge across the Sacramento around 1855. Their daughter, Elda McCloud, was the first to call a colorful local fish the Dolly Varden trout. Ewing Young's cattle drive stopped here in the 1830s, and the U.S. Exploring Expedition passed through in 1841. In the 1850s, a band of Wintu people fleeing miners on the Trinity River crossed the mountains and settled near the springs. Well-to-do Victorian travelers came to take the waters, but the resort closed by 1920 as cars changed vacation habits.

places.name: Babe Ruth in Dunsmuir
places.text: In 1924, New York Yankees stars Babe Ruth and Bob Meusel came to Dunsmuir on a barnstorming tour and played an exhibition game against the locals in the city park. That park is now home to a botanical garden along the river.
places.more: Dunsmuir City Park and Botanical Gardens covers about 10 acres. A nonprofit group of volunteers looks after the gardens. In summer the park hosts an outdoor dinner and concert called Tribute to the Trees, and the town holds festivals like Railroad Days. Dunsmuir also has a big leaguer of its own: outfielder Ray Coleman was born here.

places.name: Hedge Creek Falls
places.text: A short trail from this exit leads to a waterfall with a small cave behind it, so you can walk behind the falling water. There's also a viewing platform over the river with a view of Mount Shasta. Being so close to I-5, it's a popular stop for passing drivers.
places.more: The falls pour over the tip of an old lava flow from Mount Shasta, and the cave is a natural hollow in that thick lava, not something carved by splashing water. The original plans for I-5 would have buried the falls. Locals objected so strongly that the freeway was moved farther into the hill, at a cost of about a million dollars, so the falls are nicknamed the Million Dollar Waterfall. In October 1879, the stagecoach robber Black Bart held up the Roseburg to Redding stage near Dunsmuir, and evidence suggested he hid in this cave first. Bart wore a flour sack mask, fled on foot, and was known for being polite.

places.name: Where Shasta soda began
places.text: Just north of Dunsmuir was Shasta Springs, a summer resort on the railroad main line in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Natural springs here were the original source of the water and drinks that became the Shasta brand of soft drinks.
places.more: The resort had its own train station, an incline railway up the hillside, fountains, a kiosk and a bottling plant. It closed in the early 1950s, and the property now belongs to the Saint Germain Foundation and is closed to the public. The lower resort is gone, and blackberry bushes have overgrown its ruins. The usual route to nearby Mossbrae Falls means trespassing along the railroad tracks, and hikers were injured by trains there in 2011 and 2019.

places.name: The Cantara Loop spill
places.text: On the night of July 14, 1991, a train derailed at a horseshoe curve called the Cantara Loop, upstream from Dunsmuir, and a tank car spilled about 19,000 gallons of pesticide into the river. More than a million fish died. It's still the largest hazardous chemical spill in California history, but the river has largely recovered.
places.more: The chemical, a soil fumigant called metam sodium, left a 41-mile trail of destruction all the way to Shasta Lake. Tens of thousands of frogs and crayfish died, along with millions of insects and other small river creatures, and hundreds of thousands of willows, alders and cottonwoods eventually died too. The tank car was not labeled, and federal safety investigators said its type had a high rate of failure in accidents. At the lake, a system of aerating pipes helped break the chemical down. Crayfish and frogs still have not fully returned, but the river is again open to catch-and-release fishing all year.

places.name: McCloud, a company town
places.text: Highway 89 heads east to McCloud, a lumber company town on the southern slope of Mount Shasta. For decades the company mill supplied the homes with electricity and even steam heat. The houses passed to private owners in 1965, and the mill closed for good in 2002.
places.more: The first mill here, built in 1892, failed because hauling lumber over the hills by oxen was too hard. The McCloud River Railroad, founded in 1895, solved that problem. The McCloud River rises on the east side of Mount Shasta and runs 77 miles south to Shasta Lake. In 2006, Nestle began planning a bottled water plant using spring water from Mount Shasta; after local protests, it opened a plant in Sacramento instead. Part of downtown McCloud is on the National Register of Historic Places. A statue called Joaquin's Book stands in McCloud's Hoo Hoo Park, near where poet Joaquin Miller lived with the Wintu.

places.name: Mount Shasta trout hatchery
places.text: On Old Stage Road in Mount Shasta, the Mount Shasta Hatchery has raised trout since 1888, and the state calls it the oldest trout hatchery west of the Mississippi. It supplies most of the eggs for the state's trout hatcheries, upwards of 30 million a year. From mid-March through July, visitors can watch the eggs hatch and the baby fish grow.
places.more: The same address was once the Strawberry Valley Stage Station, where stagecoach drivers got fresh horses from 1857 until the railroad arrived in 1886. Across the road stood the Berryvale post office, whose first postmaster was Justin Sisson. He built a hotel nearby in 1865 and started his own trout hatchery in 1887. The town that grew up here was called Strawberry Valley, then Sisson, and finally Mount Shasta. The stage station site is California Historical Landmark No. 396. Trout here can grow to nearly 10 pounds, and the Sisson Museum tells the story of the hatchery and the area.

places.name: Mount Shasta City
places.text: This town was called Strawberry Valley, then Berryvale, then Sisson, after Justin Sisson, who gave the land for the railroad station. It officially became the City of Mount Shasta in 1925. It sits at about 3,600 feet, less than 9 miles from the summit, and gets nearly 103 inches of snow in a typical winter.
places.more: Justin Sisson ran the Strawberry Valley stage inn, and the railroad's completion in 1887 brought tourists, loggers and new residents. In the early 1900s, many Italian immigrants came to work in the timber industry. The city incorporated in 1905. Anita Loos, the writer behind Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, was born in Sisson in 1888. The snowiest year on record was 1952, with 349.6 inches. Shasta Abbey, a Buddhist training monastery, sits just north of town, and the first Black Bear Diner opened here in 1995.

places.name: Headwaters of the Sacramento
places.text: In Mount Shasta City Park, water pours straight out of a hillside at Big Springs. It started as glacial melt and spent more than 50 years filtering through volcanic rock. About 12 million gallons a day flow out here and help start the Sacramento River.
places.more: People fill jugs at the spring to take home, though a sign warns that the water has not been tested and may not be safe to drink. In 1901, a water wheel at Big Springs gave the town its first electricity, for a few street lights. From 1920 to 1943, the park was the summer campus of the teachers' college at Chico. The spring water flows through the Mount Shasta Hatchery and into Lake Siskiyou before joining the Sacramento. Wading and swimming in the spring are not allowed.

places.name: Mount Shasta
places.text: Mount Shasta rises to 14,179 feet. By volume, about 85 cubic miles, it is the biggest stratovolcano in the Cascade Range, and seven glaciers ring its slopes. Its last major eruption was about 3,000 years ago, and the U.S. Geological Survey rates it a very high threat volcano.
places.more: The Whitney Glacier is the longest glacier in California, and the Hotlum holds the most ice. A 2002 survey found that, unusually, Shasta's glaciers had grown since 1951, fed by heavier snowfall, though researchers warned that further warming would likely make them retreat. The first recorded climb to the summit was in 1854, and the first women reached the top in 1856. Naturalist John Muir wrote about surviving an overnight blizzard near the summit by lying in hot sulfur springs. Smaller eruptions happened as recently as about 200 years ago, and a 2019 report put the chance of an eruption by 2049 at 3.5 percent.
places.spot: Look for a huge snowy volcano with a smaller cone on its west side.

places.name: The Lemurians legend
places.text: Mount Shasta has a famous legend: a hidden city on the mountain, home to advanced beings from a lost continent called Lemuria. The story grew from a passing mention in the 1880s into a whole book in 1931. No one has ever found the city.
places.more: The idea of Lemuria began in 1864, when a zoologist proposed a sunken continent to explain why lemur fossils turned up in both Madagascar and India. Scientists dropped the idea once plate tectonics explained the puzzle. By 1925 writers described a hidden Lemurian village on Shasta, and a 1931 book by Harvey Spencer Lewis, written under a pen name, cemented the legend. Science fiction writer Robert Heinlein used it in a 1941 story. Much older are the stories of the Klamath Tribes, which tell of Skell, the Spirit of the Above-World, living on the mountain and battling Llao of Mount Mazama with hot rocks and lava.

places.name: Black Butte
places.text: The dark cone close beside the freeway is Black Butte, a cluster of lava domes that squeezed out about 9,000 to 10,000 years ago. I-5 crosses a 3,912-foot pass at its western base, called Black Butte Summit.
places.more: Over the years it has also been called Wintoon Butte, Cone Mountain, Sugar Loaf and Muir's Peak. A Forest Service fire lookout stood on top from the early 1930s until the Columbus Day Storm of 1962 destroyed it. A new lookout was used from 1963 to 1973, then lifted away by helicopter in 1975, leaving only its concrete foundation. A 2.5-mile trail climbs to the summit, where on clear days Mount McLoughlin in Oregon shows up 70 miles away. At Black Butte, the railroad's Cascade Line by way of Klamath Falls, built in the 1920s, meets the older Siskiyou Line.
places.spot: Look for a dark, rocky cone standing close to the freeway.

places.name: Mount Eddy
places.text: The big peak west of the freeway is Mount Eddy, 9,037 feet tall, the highest point in the Trinity Mountains. It's made mostly of a rock called serpentinized peridotite. Mount Eddy is the highest summit west of I-5 anywhere in the United States.
places.more: Mount Eddy is named for Olive Paddock Eddy, who is often mistakenly credited with being the first woman to climb Mount Shasta, supposedly while eight months pregnant. Harriet Eddy was actually among the first women to reach the top. Nelson Eddy came here from New York in 1856 and became a successful rancher in Shasta Valley. The Wintu name for the peak may have been Num-mel-be-le-sas-pam, west blaze mountain. The Shasta River begins on Mount Eddy's east slope. The peak belongs to the Klamath Mountains, home to about 30 kinds of conifers, one of the richest conifer forests in the world.
places.spot: Look for the tallest mountain on the west side of the freeway.

places.name: Shastina and Diller Canyon
places.text: The smaller peak on Mount Shasta's west side is Shastina, about 12,330 feet tall. That's taller than Mount Adams in Washington. The big gash down its side facing Weed is Diller Canyon, cut by hot volcanic flows, and it drops more than 7,000 vertical feet.
places.more: Shastina was built about 9,500 years ago, after the last ice age, which is why its summit crater is still intact. Its eruptions, along with those of Black Butte, sent hot flows across about 43 square miles, including much of the ground where Mount Shasta City and Weed now stand. The crater holds three small lakes, including Clarence King Lake and Sisson Lake, the highest open-air lakes in the whole Cascade Range. They rarely melt free of snow until late summer. The name Shastina simply means little Shasta.
places.spot: Look for the deep groove of Diller Canyon down the smaller peak.

places.name: A mountain of many names
places.text: The first written description of Mount Shasta came from a Spanish expedition. On May 20, 1817, Narciso Duran wrote of a very high hill, entirely covered with snow, that soldiers called Jesus Maria. The Shasta people call the mountain Waka-nunee-Tuki-wuki, and in the Karuk language it is Uytaahkoo.
places.more: Fur trapper Peter Skene Ogden of the Hudson's Bay Company recorded seeing the mountain in 1826, and in 1827 he gave the name Sasty or Sastise to Mount McLoughlin in Oregon instead. An 1839 map called this peak Rogers Peak. The name Shasta moved to this mountain in 1841, partly through the work of the United States Exploring Expedition. Where the word Shasta itself comes from is unclear. The name Yreka, though, comes from waik'a, the Shasta people's word for this mountain, meaning north mountain or white mountain.

places.name: Weed, a windy lumber town
places.text: Weed is named for Abner Weed, who found that the strong winds here were good for drying lumber. In 1897 he bought a mill and 280 acres for 400 dollars. The town motto is Weed like to welcome you, and over the years its road signs have had a habit of disappearing.
places.more: Abner Weed had been a Union soldier and was at Appomattox for Lee's surrender. In 1902 he built 30 miles of railroad from Weed to Grass Lake, and in 1904 he sold his holdings to R.A. Long of Kansas City. The mills drew many Italian immigrants, and streets in the old Italian neighborhood are named for Rome, Genoa, Como and Venice. Weed has held its Carnevale every June or July since 1954, with bocce ball tournaments. The town's water comes from Beaughan Spring, piped straight to homes. The Weed Historic Lumber Town Museum shows sawmill machinery from the early days.

places.name: Pluto's Cave
places.text: About 12 miles northeast of Weed is Pluto's Cave, a lava tube roughly 190,000 years old. A man named Nelson Cash stumbled onto it in 1863 while looking for stray cattle, and it was named for Pluto, the god of the underworld. Visitors can hike about 1,200 feet inside.
places.more: Lava tubes usually collapse quickly, but the dry climate here has helped this one survive. In October 1863, survey scientists William Brewer and Clarence King went nearly a mile in. They found bats all the way to the end and skulls of bighorn sheep near the entrance, where the roof had fallen in. King came back in 1870 and repeated an experiment from that first visit: he blew out his candle to feel the total darkness, then fired a pistol to hear the muffled boom. John Muir wrote about it too, warning that it was hard to find because its openings are level with the ground. There is evidence that people used the cave long before Europeans arrived.

places.name: A two-block highway
places.text: This exit is the end of State Route 265, North Weed Boulevard. It's only two blocks long, which makes it the second-shortest state highway in California.
places.more: Route 265 runs from U.S. 97 in Weed to the North Weed interchange on I-5. It used to be part of U.S. Route 99. For many years the route was hidden, with no signs at all. The only clue was a bridge number spray-painted on the base of the I-5 overpass: 265 overcrossing. Signs finally went up in 2005, in preparation for a full rebuild of Weed Boulevard.

places.name: Weed's wildfires
places.text: The same strong winds that dry lumber have driven wildfires through Weed. On September 15, 2014, the wind-driven Boles Fire destroyed more than 150 buildings, most of them homes, in a single day. On September 2, 2022, the Mill Fire started at the lumber mill north of town and burned the Lincoln Heights neighborhood.
places.more: Fire officials traced the Mill Fire to the mill's operations, and the company said a machine meant to cool hot ash from its wood-burning power plant may have failed. The fire destroyed 118 structures, and two people died. It raced north into Lake Shastina, and that same afternoon a second blaze, the Mountain Fire, started near Gazelle. In 2021, the Lava Fire, believed to have been started by lightning, burned more than 26,000 acres on Mount Shasta's slopes. It also damaged a railroad trestle, disrupting Amtrak's Coast Starlight for weeks.

places.name: Gazelle's antelope name
places.text: West of the freeway sits Gazelle, a tiny town of about 95 people. Its post office took the name Gazelle in 1870. A gazelle is a small African antelope, and in the 1850s a steamer called the Gazelle also ran between San Francisco and the upper Sacramento River.
places.more: Gazelle lies in the Shasta River's watershed, a dry farming valley. Most of the river's water there comes from groundwater and from irrigation runoff. On September 2, 2022, the afternoon the Mill Fire broke out in Weed, another blaze called the Mountain Fire started on Gazelle-Callahan Road, east of Gazelle Mountain. With the two fires spreading side by side, firefighting crews were stretched thin.

places.name: Old Highway 99
places.text: A two-lane county road called Old Highway 99 runs between Weed and Yreka, still in the same form it had when it was U.S. 99, the main West Coast highway before I-5. It roughly parallels the freeway, but at one point swings several miles away.
places.more: U.S. 99 was created in 1926 and ran from the Mexican border to the Canadian border. It was known as the Golden State Highway and the Main Street of California. Its end began with a 1963 bill by State Senator Randolph Collier that renumbered California's highways, and by 1968 the route was gone, replaced here by I-5. In Weed, a short piece of it survives as State Route 265. North of Yreka, old 99 became State Route 263, and much of it between Hornbrook and Oregon has been torn up or sits on private land.

places.name: The hummocks of Shasta Valley
places.text: See the little lumpy hills scattered across the flat valley? Hundreds of thousands of years ago, an older version of Mount Shasta collapsed in one of the largest landslides known on Earth. The debris spread across more than 170 square miles of Shasta Valley, and these hummocks are the pieces.
places.more: Today's Mount Shasta was built on the remains of that older volcano. The collapse sent about 6.5 cubic miles of rock flowing into Shasta Valley. The hills reach from the base of the mountain to just past Montague. The Shasta River now cuts through the 28-mile-long flow.
places.spot: Look for small lumpy hills scattered across the flat valley floor.

places.name: Hay and cattle country
places.text: Shasta Valley is one of Siskiyou County's four main farming areas. Alfalfa hay is the county's biggest field crop: in 2023, farmers cut about 175,000 tons of it from some 29,000 acres. Ranchers counted around 45,000 cattle and calves at the start of that year.
places.more: The valley lies in the rain shadow of the Klamath Mountains and gets only about 14 inches of rain a year, so its fields depend on groundwater and irrigation. Siskiyou County also counts about 445,000 acres of rangeland pasture. In 2023, its cows, steers, heifers and bulls together were worth about 112 million dollars. The county also grows wheat, barley, rye and even mint. Long before ranching, Shasta people here harvested grasshoppers by setting patches of grassland on fire and gathering the cooked insects.
places.spot: Look for hay fields and cattle grazing across the valley.

places.name: A billion strawberry plants
places.text: Siskiyou County's most valuable farm product isn't hay or cattle. It's strawberry plants. In 2023 the county grew them on more than 2,800 acres, at about 360,000 plants per acre. That adds up to roughly a billion young plants, worth about 184 million dollars.
places.more: They count as nursery crops, grown for planting rather than for berries. Nursery crops brought in about 200 million of the county's 451 million dollars in crop, livestock and timber value in 2023. The county also grew raspberry plants and garlic for planting. Its farmers harvested about 3,300 acres of potatoes, including organic ones, and 170 acres of horseradish.

places.name: Shasta Valley Wildlife Area
places.text: About five miles east, near Montague, the state's Shasta Valley Wildlife Area protects some 4,700 acres of juniper woodland, riverside forest, wetlands and fields, with Mount Shasta as its backdrop. Sandhill cranes, waterfowl, birds of prey and shorebirds all use it.
places.more: The wildlife area was set aside in 1991. It has three deep-water reservoirs, including Trout Lake, a trophy fishery for rainbow trout and largemouth bass. Deer, porcupines and coyotes live here too. During waterfowl hunting season, other visitors can come only on certain days, so it is worth checking before a visit.

places.name: State of Jefferson
places.text: On November 27, 1941, young men waving hunting rifles stopped traffic on U.S. 99 south of Yreka and handed out a proclamation of independence for the State of Jefferson. They promised to secede every Thursday until further notice. The movement's seal is a gold pan with two Xs, called the Double Cross, for feeling abandoned by both state capitals.
places.more: The plan joined Siskiyou, Del Norte and Modoc counties in California with four counties in Oregon, and Yreka was picked as the capital, thanks partly to State Senator Randolph Collier. The movement's leader, Port Orford mayor Gilbert Gable, died suddenly on December 2, 1941. Five days later came Pearl Harbor, and the rebellion fizzled as people turned to the war. The gold pan said to be the first model for the seal is on display at the Siskiyou County Museum in Yreka. The idea never fully died: in 2013, Siskiyou County supervisors voted 4 to 1 to seek withdrawal from California.

places.name: Yreka, the gold town
places.text: In March 1851, a mule packer named Abraham Thompson found gold here, and by April, 2,000 miners had arrived at what they called Thompson's Dry Diggings. The name Yreka comes from waik'a, the Shasta people's word for Mount Shasta. Mark Twain told a funnier story: a bakery sign seen backwards, BAKERY without the B, read YREKA.
places.more: Yreka is the county seat, and its brick courthouse, finished in 1857, stayed in use until 2021. The heart of downtown, along West Miner Street, is a historic district and a California Historical Landmark. The town holds Gold Rush Days every June, and its city flower is the Yreka phlox. The Karuk Tribe has housing, offices and the Rain Rock Casino on its land here, and in the Karuk language Yreka is kahtishraam. The town's history also includes hard chapters, among them two lynchings, in 1895 and 1935.

places.name: Yreka builds its own railroad
places.text: When the Southern Pacific laid its main line through Shasta Valley in the 1880s, it skipped Yreka for a shorter, more level route through Montague. So the people of Yreka built their own railroad. The Yreka Railroad opened in January 1889 and connected the town to the main line at Montague.
places.more: Montague was named for S.S. Montague, chief engineer of the Central Pacific Railroad, when the station was built in 1886 and 1887. The little Yreka line was reorganized as the Yreka Western Railroad in 1933, and in 1953 it was bought by Willis Kyle, who went on to build a group of short-line railroads. For years it also ran tourist excursions, until 2016. Today it still hauls freight such as wood chips, forest products and propane.

places.name: The Shasta River
places.text: The Shasta River starts on Mount Eddy and runs 58 miles through Shasta Valley to the Klamath. North of Yreka, the freeway crosses it, and the river then slips into a canyon. It's a spawning river for Chinook salmon, and estimates say about 80,000 adult fish once returned to it every year.
places.more: Most of its water comes from groundwater and irrigation runoff, and some is Mount Shasta snowmelt that flows out of lava tubes as springs, feeding creeks like Big Springs Creek. The valley gets only about 14 inches of rain a year. Today fewer than one in ten of those salmon still return, and recent droughts have made it hard for young fish to survive. The river also supports coho salmon and steelhead. It meets the Klamath where Highways 263 and 96 come together.

places.name: The Shasta people
places.text: Shasta Valley and the nearby Klamath River are part of the homeland of the Shasta people, and the people of the Shasta River were known as the Ahotireitsu. Women and children dove in the Klamath for mussels. Today Shasta people live in Yreka and on the Quartz Valley Indian Reservation, and on the Grand Ronde and Siletz reservations in Oregon.
places.more: Gold miners poured onto Shasta land in 1850 and 1851. In November 1851, Shasta leaders signed a treaty that promised them a reservation in Scott Valley, but it was one of 18 California treaties that the state opposed and the U.S. Senate rejected. Shasta accounts later told of beef poisoned with strychnine, served by American officials at the treaty celebration. In July 1852, miners killed 14 Shasta people in Shasta Valley in revenge for the death of a white man. In the late 1850s, Shasta families were forcibly removed to reservations in Oregon. By 1910, one anthropologist estimated only about 100 Shasta remained.

places.name: The Klamath Mountains
places.text: The rugged, forested mountains to the west are the Klamath Mountains. Their rocks began as volcanic islands and pieces of other continents out in the Pacific, some as old as 500 million years, that later crashed into North America. They hold one of the richest mixes of cone-bearing trees on Earth, about 30 kinds.
places.more: Two of those conifers, Brewer's spruce and Port Orford cedar, grow almost nowhere else. In 1969, botanists counted 17 kinds of conifers in a single square mile of the Russian Wilderness and called it the Miracle Mile. An 18th was found there in 2013, and it is now considered the richest gathering of conifers for its size in any temperate region on Earth. The mountains also hold serpentine and marble, black bears and mountain lions, and nine native species in the salmon family.
places.spot: Look for steep, forested mountain ridges to the west.

places.name: The Klamath River
places.text: The freeway crosses the Klamath River near here, where the river turns sharply south to meet I-5. Upstream, four hydroelectric dams were torn down in 2023 and 2024, the largest dam removal in American history. On October 17, 2024, a fall-run Chinook salmon was spotted in Oregon's Upper Klamath Basin, the first to reach it in more than 100 years.
places.more: The Klamath is the third-largest salmon and steelhead river on the West Coast of the lower 48 states. It is also one of only three U.S. rivers that cross the Cascade Range. Copco No. 2 came down first, in October 2023, and the last of the dams was gone in 2024, reopening about 400 miles of river to spawning salmon. In 2025, tagged Chinook were seen above Upper Klamath Lake for the first time in more than a century. That same summer, Indigenous teenagers from the region made the first canoe trip down the entire river in over 100 years.
places.spot: Look for the river below the freeway bridge.

places.name: Randolph Collier Rest Area
places.text: This rest area by the Klamath River honors State Senator Randolph Collier, who lived in Siskiyou County nearly all his life. He co-wrote the 1947 law that laid the groundwork for California's freeway system, so in a way, you're driving on his idea.
places.more: Collier served in the state Senate from 1939 to 1976 and chaired its Transportation Committee. In 1941, his support helped make Yreka the planned capital of the State of Jefferson. In 1963, his bill to simplify California's highway numbers began the end of U.S. 99. He started out as a Republican and switched to the Democratic Party in 1959, and he opposed rapid transit. A tunnel on U.S. 199, the Redwood Highway, also carries his name.

places.name: Into Karuk country
places.text: Highway 96 follows the Klamath River west into Karuk country. Karuk means upriver, and traditionally the Karuk called themselves the middle of the world people. The Karuk Tribe is one of the largest tribes in California, and the 2010 census counted about 6,100 Karuk people.
places.more: Karuk ancestral territory covers more than a million acres along the Klamath, land the tribe has never ceded. The river was once lined with more than 120 Karuk villages. Today the tribe serves its people from Happy Camp, Orleans and Yreka, and runs everything from health clinics to salmon restoration, cultural burning and dam removal work. The Karuk language is not related to any other known language. Fewer than five people spoke it fluently full-time as of 2025, and the tribe has an active program to bring it back.

places.name: Where Siskiyou got its name
places.text: Nobody is sure where the name Siskiyou comes from. One story says it was a Cree word for a bob-tailed horse. Another says Hudson's Bay Company trappers gave a river ford the French name Six Cailloux, six stones, and that the name was later borrowed for a crossing on the Klamath River near Hornbrook.
places.more: Historian Richard Mackie says a bob-tailed horse died in 1829 on Alexander McLeod's Hudson's Bay Company trip over a pass that was later named for it. Cree members of that party had been recruited far away in eastern Canada. The six stones story was argued before the California State Senate in 1852, the year Siskiyou County was created. That ford was on Oregon's Umpqua River, where six large rocks lay in the water, and trapper Stephen Meek is said to have carried the name to the Klamath. Others credit the name to the many Native nations of the region.

places.name: Hilt, the border town
places.text: Hilt has the northernmost I-5 exit in California. It grew up as a company town, first for the Northern California Lumber Company and then for the Fruit Growers Supply Company, an affiliate of Sunkist. It's named for an early settler, John Hilt.
places.more: In July 2018, the Klamathon Fire started near Hornbrook and forced Hilt to evacuate, along with Hornbrook and Colestin, Oregon. It destroyed 82 structures and killed one person before it was contained on July 21. Investigators blamed reckless burning of debris. Just north of Hilt rise the Siskiyou Mountains, the divide between the Klamath and Rogue river basins.

places.name: The 42nd parallel
places.text: The California and Oregon border follows the 42nd parallel, a line set in an 1819 treaty between the United States and Spain. When California became a state in 1850, it kept that line as its northern border. A survey around 1870 marked it with errors, creating a dispute that continues to this day.
places.more: A few miles north, in Oregon, I-5 crosses Siskiyou Summit at 4,310 feet, its highest point anywhere. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the freeway up there, and snow generally falls from November through April. Hudson's Bay Company trappers crossed these mountains on the Siskiyou Trail as early as 1827. Just east of the summit stands Pilot Rock, a volcanic plug about 25 million years old that guided pioneers coming north from California on the Applegate Trail.

zones.label: North Redding and the dam towns
zones.text: Here Redding's northern edge meets the city of Shasta Lake, which grew from the camps of the people who built Shasta Dam, a few miles west.

seasons.summer: Summers here are hot and dry, with big swings between daytime highs and nighttime lows.

zones.label: Shasta Lake
zones.text: The freeway crosses California's largest reservoir, whose steep shores are covered with tall evergreens and manzanita. In drought years, old highway bridges and railroad tunnels show above the water.

seasons.summer: Summer is the busy season at Bridge Bay, the lake's largest marina, and Lakehead can gain more than 1,500 seasonal residents.

zones.label: Sacramento River canyon
zones.text: A steep, forested canyon where the river, the railroad and I-5 squeeze side by side, past old stage stops and Gold Rush camps.

seasons.winter: North of Redding, snow can fall at higher elevations from fall to spring, and Caltrans sometimes requires chains.

zones.label: Castle Crags and Dunsmuir
zones.text: Granite spires rise west of the freeway, and an old railroad town fills the canyon bottom. Dunsmuir gets about 63 inches of rain and snow a year, about three and a half times as much as Yreka or Medford.

seasons.winter: More than half of Dunsmuir's yearly rain and snow falls in December, January and February.
seasons.spring: Dunsmuir's last freeze comes around April 24 in an average year.
seasons.summer: In summer, Dunsmuir stocks the river in town with trophy rainbow trout up to 14 pounds.
seasons.fall: The first freeze usually arrives around October 20.

zones.label: Mount Shasta and Black Butte
zones.text: The canyon opens onto the foot of the volcano, with the city of Mount Shasta, the dark cone of Black Butte and Black Butte Summit at 3,912 feet.

seasons.winter: Mount Shasta City averages nearly 103 inches of snow a year, and in February 1959 the old Ski Bowl on the mountain got 15.75 feet in one storm, a U.S. record.
seasons.spring: From mid-March through July, visitors can watch trout eggs hatch at the Mount Shasta Hatchery.
seasons.summer: Climbers head for Mount Shasta's summit from late April into October.

zones.label: Weed, lumber and wind
zones.text: Weed grew up around lumber mills, helped by strong winds that dried the boards. Hot flows from Shastina's eruptions once covered the ground here, and recent wildfires have left their marks.

seasons.summer: Weed holds its Carnevale, with bocce ball tournaments, each June or July.

zones.label: Shasta Valley
zones.text: A wide, dry valley in the rain shadow of the Klamath Mountains, dotted with the hummocks of an ancient landslide, with hay fields, cattle and juniper.

seasons.summer: Summer rain almost never falls here, except for an occasional thunderstorm.
seasons.winter: Winters are cool to cold, with fairly frequent snow.

zones.label: Yreka gold country
zones.text: Gold Rush country around the county seat, with the Klamath Mountains rising to the west and the Shasta River cutting north toward the Klamath.

seasons.summer: Yreka holds Gold Rush Days every June.
seasons.winter: Yreka averages only about 12 inches of snow a year, mostly from November through February.

zones.label: Klamath River to the Oregon line
zones.text: Below the old Iron Gate Dam site, the Klamath runs through an arid valley of farms and ranches before bending south to meet I-5. To the north rise the Siskiyou Mountains, the divide between the Klamath and the Rogue.

seasons.fall: Fall-run Chinook salmon now swim past here into Oregon; the first one reached the Upper Klamath Basin on October 17, 2024.
seasons.winter: Just over the Oregon line, Siskiyou Summit usually gets snow from November through April.

trivia.q: How long was the conveyor belt that carried rock to build Shasta Dam?
trivia.why: It ran 9.5 miles from Redding to the dam site, then the largest conveyor belt system in the world.

trivia.q: What lies about 400 feet under Shasta Lake?
choices: The copper mining town of Kennett
trivia.why: Kennett was completely underwater by 1944 as the lake filled behind Shasta Dam.

trivia.q: What is the Pit River named for?
choices: Pits its people dug for homes and to trap game
trivia.why: The name comes from the pits the Pit River people dug for winter homes and as traps for game that came to drink at the river.

trivia.q: About how high above the old Pit River was the Pit River Bridge built?
trivia.why: It stands about 500 feet above the old riverbed, though a full lake comes within about 40 feet of the bridge.

trivia.q: Which baseball legend played an exhibition game in Dunsmuir in 1924?
trivia.why: Babe Ruth and Bob Meusel played the locals in the city park on a barnstorming tour.

trivia.q: Which soft drink brand got its start at natural springs just north of Dunsmuir?
trivia.why: Springs at the old Shasta Springs resort were the original source of the Shasta brand of soft drinks.

trivia.q: How much snow fell at the old Mount Shasta Ski Bowl in a single February 1959 storm?
trivia.why: The 15.75 feet that fell from February 13 to 19, 1959, set the U.S. record for snow in one storm.
Mount Shasta rises 14,179 feet, the second-highest peak in the Cascades.

trivia.q: Why did Abner Weed pick this spot for his lumber mill?
trivia.why: He found that the area's strong winds helped dry lumber.

trivia.q: In 1941, State of Jefferson rebels promised to secede how often?
trivia.why: Their proclamation said they would secede every Thursday until further notice.

trivia.q: According to Mark Twain, where did the name Yreka come from?
trivia.why: Twain said a bakery sign seen from behind read YREKA, but the name really comes from the Shasta word for Mount Shasta.

trivia.q: How many hydroelectric dams were torn down on the Klamath River in 2023 and 2024?
trivia.why: Four dams came out, the largest dam removal in U.S. history.
